children: Gold has had a volatile start to September. After touching a recent high of Rs 1,63,229 per 10 grams on August 24, prices slipped sharply, trading between roughly Rs 1.52 lakh and Rs 1.59 lakh per 10 grams during September 1-3.
Prices have recovered somewhat since then, but the sudden fall after gold's strong rally raises a simple question for investors: how unusual is it for gold to correct sharply from its highs?

Data going back to 1980 shows that sizeable declines within a year have been a regular feature of gold's journey. In fact, gold's average intra-year drawdown over this period has been around 13 percent, according to the FundsIndia Research.
And here's the interesting part: a sharp fall during the year did not necessarily mean gold finished that year in the red.
What does a 13% drawdown actually mean?
A drawdown simply measures how much the price of an asset falls from an earlier peak.
So, if gold climbs to Rs 1 lakh and subsequently falls to Rs 87,000 before recovering, that represents a 13 percent drawdown.
The FundsIndia data shows that corrections around the 10-15 percent mark have occurred repeatedly over the past four-and-a-half decades.
For instance, gold saw intra-year drawdowns of 13 percent in 1984, 12 percent in 1985, 15 percent in 1993, 13 percent in 2004, 14 percent in 2007 and 12 percent in 2009.
More recently, the pattern has continued. Gold saw drawdowns of around 15 percent in 2020, 13 percent in 2021, 15 percent in 2022 and 10 percent in 2023.
Gold has seen much steeper falls too
Some years were considerably more painful.

The biggest drawdown in the dataset came in 1980, when gold fell as much as 40 percent from its peak during the year. It saw a 25 percent drawdown in 1981, 23 percent in both 1982 and 1983, and 22 percent in 2006.
During the global financial crisis in 2008, gold corrected as much as 20 percent within the year. In 2013, the drawdown was even steeper at 24 percent.
In other words, a double-digit fall in gold is hardly unprecedented.
A fall during the year doesn't necessarily mean a negative year
Perhaps the more interesting part of the data is what happened after these corrections.
Despite experiencing intra-year declines, gold ended the calendar year with positive returns 78 percent of the time over the period covered by the FundsIndia analysis.

Take 2008. Gold suffered a drawdown of as much as 20 percent during the year, but still finished with a 29 percent calendar-year return. In 2003, it fell as much as 17 percent at one point but ended the year up 25 percent.

The same pattern can be seen more recently. Gold's maximum drawdown was 15 percent in 2020, yet it finished the year up 28 percent. In 2023, it corrected as much as 10 percent during the year but ended with a 15 percent gain.
So, what does history tell investors?
The historical numbers don't tell us whether the current correction is over, whether gold will fall further, or where prices will end 2026.
What they do show is that corrections have been a normal part of gold's long-term price movement, including in years that eventually delivered positive returns.

That distinction becomes particularly relevant after a strong rally. A fall from a recent high can look dramatic when viewed over a few days, but the longer history shows that gold's journey has rarely been a straight line.

title: Gold has fallen sharply from its recent high. But how unusual is a 10-15% correction?
